domain_assessment.domain: Enterprise design-systems procurement and accessibility-compliance implementation
domain_assessment.role: Design systems lead for a platform organization, managing three designers and two engineers while coordinating with two customer-facing product squads
domain_assessment.objective: Select and deploy an external component-library solution quickly enough to help meet a WCAG 2.2 AA compliance deadline and reduce internal contrast and focus-state remediation work
domain_assessment.incident_type: Time-constrained vendor evaluation, licensing, rollout planning, and post-audit implementation decision involving accessibility defects in an adopted design-system library

decision_points.summary: After a vendor demo centered on a polished accordion component, the participant recommends a broad pilot of LumenKit's full token set across both squads rather than a narrower component-by-component test.
evidence_before: Legal requires WCAG 2.2 AA coverage across two customer-facing squads within about ten weeks.
The internal component library has known contrast and focus-state debt.
The vendor spends most of a roughly forty-minute demo on one accordion component's motion, keyboard handling, and graceful degradation.
The vendor mentions AA-compliant color defaults.
The participant knows competitors use LumenKit and that it has industry recognition.
evidence_after: The participant tells the VP to move quickly and pilot the full token set.
Squad leads express interest but require pricing before allocating engineering time.
goals_constraints: Avoid months of internal remediation work.
Make an adoption-scope decision before independent token-level validation.
alternatives: Pilot the full token set across both squads.
Pilot selected components or tokens narrowly.
Conduct independent contrast checks before selecting pilot scope.
Continue internal remediation without adopting the vendor library.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant uses the demo's high overall quality impression to justify broad pilot scope and separately infers likely token quality from the observed accordion quality, reputation cues, and vendor claims.
decision_points.time_pressure: High; the compliance objective has an approximately ten-week deadline.
decision_points.uncertainty: High; the participant has not directly inspected the color or elevation tokens or run independent contrast checks.

decision_points.summary: The participant recommends the Enterprise licensing tier and sets an aggressive four-week rollout period based on comparative tier framing and confidence in personal oversight.
evidence_before: Procurement requires a recommendation within two weeks.
Basic offers five components and no support.
Team offers twelve components and limited support for a price close to Enterprise.
Enterprise offers the full library and dedicated support.
The implementation depends on two squads whose release calendars have not been formally confirmed.
evidence_after: One squad subsequently reports an unrelated release freeze that cannot accommodate the timeline.
goals_constraints: Choose an economically viable license tier.
Secure enough components and vendor support.
Move implementation quickly enough to preserve the overall compliance timeline.
alternatives: A scoped custom build or needs-based alternative analysis.
Confirm squad feasibility before committing to a rollout date.
Use a conditional or phased rollout schedule.
decision_points.decision_basis: Enterprise is judged mainly by contrast with the unattractive Team tier rather than an independent needs-based assessment. The timeline is set because the participant believes close personal management can overcome unconfirmed squad-calendar constraints.
decision_points.time_pressure: High; procurement has a two-week decision window and the broader accessibility deadline remains active.
decision_points.uncertainty: Moderate to high; actual component needs, comparative alternatives, and squad release constraints are not fully verified.

decision_points.summary: After an internal accessibility audit identifies contrast failures, the participant interprets them as likely implementation-specific and chooses to continue token customization rather than pause or revert to legacy components.
evidence_before: Seven weeks into the process, an internal audit finds contrast-ratio failures in three of five tested components.
The participant had publicly told the VP and squad leads that LumenKit would solve most contrast problems out of the box.
Vendor documentation states that the library is AA compliant.
More than forty engineering hours have already been invested in token customization.
Legacy components have remediated contrast values for the affected screens.
evidence_after: The participant continues refining LumenKit customization.
The VP requests a written explanation for the compliance file.
One squad lead independently reverts affected screens to legacy components.
goals_constraints: Resolve identified accessibility failures before the deadline.
Explain the discrepancy for compliance documentation.
Determine whether defects originate in vendor tokens or local theming.
alternatives: Continue refining the customized LumenKit tokens.
Pause implementation and independently retest vendor defaults without local theming.
Revert affected screens to legacy components.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant initially gives more weight to an explanation that preserves the prior public endorsement—local theming rather than vendor tokens—and then explicitly cites already-spent engineering hours as a reason not to revert.
decision_points.time_pressure: High; only about three weeks remain before the original ten-week compliance deadline.
decision_points.uncertainty: High; the participant does not conduct the diagnostic retest required to separate local-theming effects from vendor-token defects.

decision_points.summary: Three weeks before the deadline, the participant recommends retaining the largely current LumenKit implementation, including its tokens, rather than adopting a hybrid option described as technically cleaner.
evidence_before: The hybrid option would preserve LumenKit motion and layout components while sourcing color and elevation tokens internally.
The participant says the hybrid option directly addresses the token problem and is arguably the cleanest fix.
The current implementation is already running and understood by both squads.
The teams have familiarity with the current setup's behavior.
Only three weeks remain before the deadline.
evidence_after: The participant recommends continuing largely as implemented rather than moving to the hybrid structure.
goals_constraints: Avoid operational disruption across two squads.
Select an implementation arrangement that teams can execute under time pressure.
alternatives: Expand the current LumenKit implementation organization-wide.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant explicitly treats the familiar current arrangement as a safer known quantity and gives greater weight to team familiarity than to the hybrid option's stronger technical case.
decision_points.time_pressure: High; the final selection occurs three weeks before the deadline.
decision_points.uncertainty: Moderate; the hybrid's technical advantage is acknowledged, but its actual transition burden is not comparatively assessed.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “After that call I told my VP I thought we should move fast and pilot the full token set across both squads rather than cherry-picking pieces, because the overall quality bar felt high enough that a narrower test seemed like it'd just slow us down.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Participant's initial account of the vendor demo and immediate pilot-scope recommendation; reinforced by the later demo-order counterfactual probe.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The vendor's lengthy, vivid, positive accordion demonstration establishes a favorable overall evaluative frame before token-level evidence is reviewed. The participant applies that broad frame to the pilot-scope judgment. The later statement that seeing contrast-ratio data first might have led to a narrower pilot supports a presentation-order effect rather than merely general enthusiasm.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: A broad pilot can be a rational integration test under a ten-week compliance deadline, particularly if isolated component testing would not reveal system-level implementation issues. The occurrence remains supported because the participant explicitly says the demo's overall quality bar made narrow testing seem unnecessarily slow.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None. The interview contains both the initial framing trace and a counterfactual probe that identifies demo order as potentially decision-relevant.

revision.location: Decision point 1, immediately after the accordion-focused vendor demonstration.
revision.current_defect: No material defect. The general evaluative-frame transfer is distinguishable from the specific cross-attribute inference supporting the halo-effect occurrence.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the current broad-pilot rationale and the later counterfactual question about whether contrast data appearing first would have changed pilot scope.
preserve: The forty-minute accordion-centered demo.
The broad full-token-set pilot recommendation.
The separate explicit contrast-token inference used for the halo-effect occurrence.
The demo-order counterfactual.
avoid_creating: Do not replace the broad evaluative-frame language with a token-specific inference, because that would merge this occurrence with cb_02.
Do not add a second pilot-scope decision elsewhere in the interview.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “But the accordion was so well executed, and given the awards and the fact that two competitors already ship with it, I figured the token layer was probably in similarly good shape.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Follow-up answer after the interviewer asks whether color and elevation tokens had been reviewed directly.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant explicitly infers quality in an unrelated, unverified attribute—color and elevation token quality and compliance—from the observed quality of motion, keyboard handling, and graceful degradation in a single accordion component, supplemented by favorable reputation cues.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: A vendor's performance on one component and its market reputation can be weakly informative about general engineering quality. They do not establish contrast compliance in unreviewed tokens, particularly when no independent contrast testing has been performed.

revision.location: Decision point 1, answer regarding the unreviewed color and elevation token layer.
revision.current_defect: No material defect. The evidence directly states both the unverified attribute and the cross-attribute inference.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the explicit distinction between the polished accordion and the untested token layer.
preserve: The participant's admission that no independent contrast checks had occurred.
The observed accordion qualities.
The vendor awards and competitor-adoption cues.
The inference that the token layer was therefore probably similarly good.
avoid_creating: Do not introduce validated token-level accessibility results before the participant makes this inference.
Do not remove the specific reference to token quality, because a generic positive vendor impression would weaken the halo mechanism.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “Team was a bad deal — you're paying almost Enterprise money for a fraction of the components and worse support. Enterprise looked obviously better sitting next to that. I didn't really run Enterprise's cost against, say, a scoped custom build or against our actual component needs in isolation.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Participant's explanation of why Enterprise appeared to be the clear licensing choice.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The Team tier functions as a relatively dominated middle option: it costs nearly as much as Enterprise while offering fewer components and weaker support. The participant explicitly says Enterprise appeared attractive because it was compared with Team and acknowledges not conducting an independent value assessment against actual needs or external alternatives.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Enterprise may genuinely offer superior value if its incremental cost above Team is small and dedicated support is operationally important. The bias mechanism is nevertheless supported because the participant identifies relative contrast with Team, rather than an independent cost-benefit analysis, as the central basis for the selection.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None. Intentional vendor construction of Team as a sales decoy is not necessary to establish a participant-level decoy-effect mechanism.

revision.current_defect: No material defect. The participant explicitly identifies Team as the comparison point and discloses the absence of an isolated value assessment.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the relative-price and relative-feature contrast between Team and Enterprise, together with the omitted comparison against actual component needs.
preserve: The three-tier structure.
The near-price relationship between Team and Enterprise.
The procurement timing constraint.
The lack of independent cost comparison with scoped internal remediation.
avoid_creating: Do not add a complete needs-based financial model demonstrating Enterprise is independently optimal.
Do not remove Team from the account or make Basic the sole unfavorable alternative.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “I figured with me driving it closely day to day, we'd make it work regardless of their existing release calendars.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Rollout-timeline discussion, after the participant confirms that neither dependent squad had formally committed to the four-week window.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant believes personal involvement and daily coordination can ensure a rollout outcome despite material determinants outside personal control: two other squads' release schedules and an unverified release freeze. The phrase “regardless of their existing release calendars” makes the external-control attribution explicit.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Hands-on leadership and daily coordination can reduce integration risk. They cannot eliminate pre-existing calendar constraints or release freezes when the participant has not verified squad capacity or authority to alter their schedules.

revision.location: Decision point 2, participant's justification for setting the four-week rollout timeline.
revision.current_defect: No material defect. The transcript directly connects confidence in personal oversight to an outcome materially controlled by unconfirmed external dependencies.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the lack of formal squad confirmation, the participant's confidence in daily management, and the subsequently revealed release freeze.
preserve: The four-week target.
The participant's active personal-management role.
The two dependent squads and their independent calendars.
The later discovery of the release freeze.
avoid_creating: Do not give the participant authority to override release freezes or reallocate squad capacity.
Do not reduce the episode to mere failure to ask about calendars; the unsupported control attribution must remain observable.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “Part of why that explanation felt like the natural one to reach for first was that I'd already told the VP and both squad leads LumenKit would solve most of our contrast problems out of the box, so ‘it's our theming, not their tokens’ sat better with what I'd already said than the alternative did.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Participant's first interpretation of the audit discrepancy, immediately after recalling the prior public endorsement.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The audit creates a conflict between the participant's earlier public commitment and new evidence that vendor-associated tokens fail contrast requirements. The participant explicitly states that the explanation preserving the prior commitment felt more acceptable than the contrary interpretation. This is belief-consistency reasoning rather than merely a technical hypothesis because the participant ties the weighting of the hypothesis to what had already been represented to others.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Local theming could genuinely alter contrast outcomes and make an implementation-specific explanation technically plausible. The occurrence is supported because the participant separately admits that its psychological attractiveness derived from preserving consistency with a prior public statement, while declining to conduct the independent retest needed to discriminate between explanations.

revision.location: Decision point 3, participant's first interpretation of the accessibility audit.
revision.current_defect: No material defect. The revised account makes the connection between prior public commitment and preferential interpretation of disconfirming evidence directly observable.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the explicit statement that the theming explanation fit better with what the participant had already told the VP and squad leads.
preserve: The audit failures in three of five tested components.
The vendor's AA-compliance documentation.
The prior public endorsement.
The absence of an independent out-of-box retest.
The separate sunk-cost rationale for continued customization.
avoid_creating: Do not add language implying intentional deception or certain knowledge that vendor tokens were defective.
Do not use an explicit textbook bias label in the dialogue.
Do not move the forty-hour investment rationale into this answer, because that would merge cb_05 with cb_06.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “We'd already put in over forty engineering hours customizing the tokens to fit our theming, so I decided we should keep refining rather than pause or fall back to legacy.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Participant's decision following the audit; reinforced by the subsequent statement that reverting would mean writing off prior hours.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant treats irrecoverable past customization work as a reason to continue rather than make a forward-looking comparison among continued refinement, hybrid adoption, and legacy reversion. This occurs despite an available legacy fallback with remediated contrast values and newly disconfirming audit evidence.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Previously completed customization work might lower future completion cost if the participant had evidence that only a small amount of remediation remained. The transcript does not provide that forward-looking comparison; instead, it explicitly treats writing off already-spent effort as the reason continuation feels more efficient.

revision.location: Decision point 3, continue-versus-revert choice after the audit.
revision.current_defect: No material defect. The prior-hours justification is explicit, backward-looking, and distinct from the participant's effort to preserve the earlier public endorsement.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the forty-plus engineering-hours reference, the available legacy fallback, and the participant's concern about writing off the prior work.
preserve: The audit findings.
The legacy components' existing remediated contrast values.
The separate belief-consistency interpretation in cb_05.
The hybrid option's later role in the final decision.
avoid_creating: Do not replace the past-investment justification with a quantified forward-looking implementation estimate.
Do not repeat the forty-hour rationale as the primary basis for rejecting the hybrid option at decision point 4.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “Even with the hybrid's technical case being reasonably strong, sticking with what we already had running felt like the safer, known quantity this close to the deadline — everyone on both squads already understood how the current setup behaved, and that familiarity mattered more to me in the moment than moving to an arrangement that was objectively cleaner but still new to the team.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Final rollout recommendation, after the hybrid option has been described as directly solving the token issue and as arguably the cleanest technical fix.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant explicitly favors the existing arrangement because it is already running, known, and familiar to the squads, despite acknowledging that the hybrid arrangement is objectively cleaner and technically stronger. The reasoning relies on continuity and familiarity rather than on past hours spent or protection of the earlier public endorsement.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Team familiarity can be a legitimate near-deadline implementation consideration. The occurrence is supported because the participant openly states that familiarity outweighed a technically superior alternative without providing a comparative assessment that establishes the hybrid transition as infeasible or materially riskier.

revision.location: Decision point 4, final choice between current LumenKit implementation, hybrid implementation, and legacy reversion.
revision.current_defect: No material defect. The account identifies continuity and team familiarity as the decisive factors and keeps them separate from sunk-cost and cognitive-dissonance rationales.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the contrast between the hybrid option's objectively cleaner technical case and the participant's preference for the familiar current setup.
preserve: The hybrid option's direct solution to the token problem.
The hybrid option's retention of LumenKit motion and layout work.
The three-week deadline.
The separate forty-hour sunk-cost episode.
The separate prior-endorsement episode.
avoid_creating: Do not reintroduce documentation, training investment, or prior-hours write-off as the main reason for staying with the current arrangement.
Do not portray the hybrid option as technically inferior or impossible to execute.
Do not add a new concern about defending the earlier public endorsement at this decision point.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “LumenKit came up because a couple of competitors use it and it's picked up some industry recognition.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: Competitor adoption and industry recognition are favorable social cues that may have increased the library's apparent legitimacy before direct technical verification.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Competitor usage and industry recognition are legitimate early screening signals in vendor discovery. The participant does not explicitly say that imitation of competitors, rather than the demo and compliance objective, caused the pilot decision.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “I didn't request an independent re-test of the vendor's out-of-box tokens without our theming applied to actually separate those two possibilities.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The participant gives early preference to an explanation consistent with the prior endorsement and does not seek the discriminating evidence needed to test the preferred explanation.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The participant may simply have lacked time or followed an incomplete technical diagnostic process. In this interview, the more specific and better-supported interpretation is cognitive dissonance because the participant expressly ties the favored explanation to the prior public statement.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “I set four weeks. Aggressive, but I was going to be hands-on managing the integration personally.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The four-week schedule may reflect an underestimate of external coordination and release-calendar constraints.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The account lacks base-rate information, comparable rollout estimates, task decomposition, or evidence of systematic underestimation. The stronger and more specific supported mechanism is illusory control over external dependencies.

nonbias_cues.cue: The ten-week WCAG 2.2 AA deadline and desire to avoid months of remediation.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: These are real organizational constraints and legitimate motivations for seeking an external solution. Deadline pressure alone does not establish distorted reasoning.

nonbias_cues.cue: No direct contrast testing before the initial pilot recommendation.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Incomplete information or omitted verification is not itself a cognitive bias. It supports the halo-effect finding only because the participant then makes an explicit cross-attribute inference from unrelated positive evidence.

nonbias_cues.cue: The later discovery of a squad release freeze.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The release freeze is an external operational constraint, not bias evidence. It provides context showing why the participant's claimed control over the rollout was unwarranted.
A failed accessibility audit does not establish any bias by itself. The relevant evidence is the participant's interpretation of the audit and the subsequent continuation decision.

nonbias_cues.cue: The possibility that local theming altered contrast behavior.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: This is a technically plausible hypothesis. It becomes evidence of cognitive dissonance only because the participant says that explanation was more attractive because it fit the earlier public endorsement.

nonbias_cues.cue: Squad familiarity with the current implementation near a deadline.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Familiarity can be a valid operational consideration in a deadline-sensitive rollout. It supports status quo bias here because the participant explicitly lets familiarity outweigh a technically cleaner alternative without a comparative transition-risk assessment.

causal_claims.claim: The accordion-first demo framing contributed to the participant's broad pilot recommendation.
causal_claims.evidence: The participant says the demo created a sufficiently high overall quality bar to justify a full-token-set pilot and later says token-level data presented first might have prompted a narrower pilot.
causal_claims.assessment: Moderately supported as a retrospective causal account. The mechanism is presentation-order framing, but the counterfactual remains self-reported and probabilistic.

causal_claims.claim: The Team tier increased Enterprise's attractiveness through relative comparison.
causal_claims.evidence: The participant says Enterprise looked obviously better sitting next to Team and states that Enterprise was not evaluated against actual component needs or scoped internal alternatives.
causal_claims.assessment: Supported as a proximal comparative-choice account. The evidence does not establish that the vendor deliberately designed Team as a decoy, but seller intent is not required for the observed participant-level decoy mechanism.

causal_claims.claim: Personal oversight would allow the four-week rollout to succeed despite squad schedules.
causal_claims.evidence: The participant states that close daily management would make the timeline work regardless of calendars; one squad then reports an unaccounted-for release freeze.
causal_claims.assessment: The participant's causal control belief is directly evidenced and is inconsistent with the unverified external dependency structure. The subsequent freeze does not prove that management was worthless, but it does demonstrate that it could not guarantee the outcome.

causal_claims.claim: The audit failures were caused by local theming rather than vendor tokens.
causal_claims.evidence: The participant proposes the hypothesis but does not request an independent retest of unthemed vendor defaults.
causal_claims.assessment: Not established. This remains an untested causal hypothesis. The interview appropriately identifies the specific diagnostic action that would have separated the competing explanations.

causal_claims.claim: Continuing customization was more efficient than reverting.
causal_claims.evidence: The participant grounds the decision in avoiding the loss of forty-plus hours already spent.
causal_claims.assessment: Weak as a forward-looking causal or economic claim. Prior effort is unrecoverable and does not by itself show that continued refinement has lower incremental cost, lower compliance risk, or a greater likelihood of meeting the deadline.

causal_claims.claim: The current arrangement was safer than the hybrid option.
causal_claims.evidence: The participant describes the current arrangement as a known quantity and says team familiarity outweighed the hybrid's objectively cleaner technical case.
causal_claims.assessment: Plausible as an operational-risk perception but incompletely assessed. The interview demonstrates a continuity preference but does not establish through comparative evidence that the hybrid transition was actually more hazardous.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Competitor adoption and industry recognition may be treated as evidence of token-level accessibility quality.
correlation_causation_risks.why_it_matters: These signals can correlate with broad vendor legitimacy but do not establish compliance for unreviewed color and elevation tokens in the participant's specific implementation.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Vendor documentation is treated as evidence against the internal audit.
correlation_causation_risks.why_it_matters: The documentation and audit could concern different configurations, especially themed versus out-of-box tokens. Neither source resolves the causal origin of the failures without a controlled unthemed retest.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Prior implementation hours are used as evidence that continuation is more efficient.
correlation_causation_risks.why_it_matters: Past effort does not indicate the incremental work required, probability of successful remediation, or relative value of legacy and hybrid alternatives.

causal_audit.changed_variable: Vendor demo framing order: the observed sequence presents the flagship accordion component before contrast-ratio token data, while the counterfactual asks whether token-level contrast data appearing first would have changed the participant's pilot-scope decision.
causal_audit.explanation: The interview's presentation-order counterfactual changes only the vendor-demo information sequence and does not introduce a second causal change. The participant's response is appropriately qualified—“possibly” and “might”—rather than asserting certainty. The proposed direction of effect is coherent: seeing contrast evidence before a polished flagship demonstration could plausibly have changed pilot scope while leaving the deadline, tiers, squads, audit, and invested hours constant.

global_revision_constraints: No occurrence-level revision is required because all seven requested instances are independently supported.
Preserve the distinction between priming as generalized demo-order framing and halo effect as a specific inference from observed accordion quality to unverified token quality.
Preserve the distinction between cognitive dissonance as evidence interpretation shaped by a prior public commitment and sunk cost bias as continuation justified by irrecoverable engineering effort.
Preserve the distinction between status quo bias as preference for a familiar existing arrangement and sunk cost bias as concern about abandoned prior investment.

If future edits are made for naturalness, retain the direct evidence connecting the prior public endorsement to the preferred theming explanation and connecting team familiarity to rejection of the technically cleaner hybrid option.
Do not add unsupported claims that the vendor intentionally designed the Team tier as a decoy; the current participant-level comparative mechanism is sufficient.
Do not alter more than the demo-information order in the stated counterfactual.
